Purnell, Jr. (ed.), Miao and Yao Linguistic Studies: Selected Articles in Chinese, 83-110. Data Paper 88. Ithaca, NY: Southeast Asia Program, Department of Asian Studies, Cornell University.
tone_statements.quote: For example, tones 1, 3, and 7 of Pai suo (in Ch'ang shun), tones 3 and 5 of Yüeh k'uan (in Wang mou), tones 3 and 7 of Yu chien (in Lo tien), tones 5 and 7 of Hsi kuan (in P'ing t'ang), and tone 5 of P'ing yen (in Lo tien) all have split into two tones on the basis of the feature of aspiration. It is just that in these dialects the pattern is not so symmetrical as that in Tsung ti, Szu ta chai, Hsien ch'ang, and Hsiao miao chai. Examples are given in Chart 3 to Chart 7. [...] Chart 14. sources.note: Orthography for Central Mashan (Dadiba, Zongdi): initials, finals, 11 tones; a full-text search for stress/accent 重音/轻声/轻读/重读 finds nothing. Central variety, not Southern.

sources.citation: Heal, Sarah. 2020. Grammar Sketch of Mashan Miao. SIL e-Books 74. Dallas, Texas: SIL International. viii+75 pp. (data from speaker WZ = Southern vernacular [hma] and LY = Central [hmm])
sources.tag: read: silent on stress
sources.access_detail: a digital copy (available on request); access check: not located online or in the libraries checked
sources.note: Nothing. It is a Role-and-Reference-Grammar syntax sketch; the only phonological content is sec.1.2 p.6-7 ('The tonal system of Mashan Miao is one of the most complex (Mortensen 2013)'), sec.1.4 p.8 ('Mashan Miao is an isolating language.. Many words are monosyllabic'), and Appendix C pp.71-72, consonant/vowel/diphthong/tone tables for the Southern vernacular (Table C.4: 9 tones, pitch 43 22 54 31 34 24 33 212 11). The word 'stress' does not occur anywhere in the text (a full-text search for stress/accent: only 'intonation pause' in the RRG theory section and 'Pitch' in Table C.4).

sources.note: Lists 'Southern Mashan Hmong' under CHUANQIANDIAN, then (Accent information): 'Hmong-Mien is usually described as being exclusively tonal, but that does not imply that the languages in this family couldn't be accentual as well, cf. Chinese. Unfortunately, we did not have access to sources that would allow us to elaborate on this point.' Family-level, second-hand, no data on this language.

sources.citation: Mortensen, David R. 2006. Logical and substantive scales in phonology. PhD dissertation, UC Berkeley (sec.3.2.3 'Mashan dialects', pp.84ff); Mortensen 2013. Tonally conditioned vowel raising in Shuijingping Mang. JEAL 22(3):189-216.
sources.tag: read: silent on stress
sources.note: Central Mashan (Shuijingping) and Xinzhai (Wangmo) tone sandhi and tone-vowel interaction; a full-text search for stress/accent finds no statement about Mashan word stress (the 'iambic stress' remark on p.247 of the dissertation concerns Hmong proper, not Mashan). Xinzhai (Wangmo) is grouped with the Mashan dialects via Xian 1990 and Niederer 1998.

sources.citation: 王辅世 (Wang Fushi) 主编. 1985. 苗语简志 [Miaoyu jianzhi]. 北京: 民族出版社.
sources.tag: read: silent on stress
sources.note: p.104-105 lists '麻山次方言.. (4) 南部土语使用人数约有七千。通行在贵州省望谟县麻山、乐宽等地' (Southern vernacular c.7,000 speakers, Mashan and Lekuan, Wangmo county); p.6 '麻山次方言因古苗语声母的送气与否，四个阴调全部或部分地各分为两调'; p.106 '麻山次方言变调时，韵母也随之改变' (tone sandhi changes the rhyme). The phonology chapter describes Dananshan (Chuanqiandian) only; the sole 轻声 (unstressed/light-tone) remark, p.12, is about Layiping (Xiangxi) prefixes. Silent on Mashan/Southern Mashan word stress.

sources.note: For the 1956-57 survey point Yüeh k'uan 乐宽, Wang mou 望谟 (Southern Mashan) Chart 14 gives 7 tones with values T1 33, T2 45, T3X 54 / T3Y 44, T4 24, T5X 54 / T5Y 44, T6 33, T7 13, T8 31 (so T1=T6, T3X=T5X, T3Y=T5Y); p.87 states that yin tones 3 and 5 have split by proto-aspiration (X = plain initials 54, Y = aspirated initials 44), with word lists in Chart 4 p.93 (e.g. 'tail' tu 54 vs 'bone' ts'ei 44). Comparative article on initial-tone co-occurrence in 20 Miao points; no sandhi or phonetic detail for this point.
